# Objectives

.align{center}
  .container width:{75%}
    .box title:{By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:} background:{.lightblue}
      **Aquifer Classification:**
      - Define **aquifers** as the fundamental unit of groundwater hydrology
      - Distinguish between **unconfined**, **confined**, and **perched** aquifers
      - Classify confining beds: **aquifuge**, **aquiclude**, **aquitard**, and real-world **aquitardifers**

      **Aquifer Properties:**
      - Calculate **transmissivity** ($ T = Kb $) and **storativity** ($ S $)
      - Explain **specific storage**, **specific yield**, and **specific retention**
      - Compare storage mechanisms in confined vs unconfined aquifers

# Objectives
.align{center}
    .container width:{75%}
        .box title:{By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:} background:{.lightblue}
            **Aquifer Systems:**
            - Identify major aquifer types: **basin-fill**, **fluvial**, **semiconsolidated**, **sandstone**, and **carbonate-rock** aquifers
            - Understand how depositional environments control aquifer properties
            - Recognise **karst features**: sinkholes, solution conduits, and cave systems
            - Apply concepts to real-world examples (Dakota Sandstone, Gulf Coast, Floridan aquifer system)

# Introduction

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    - Just as the **catchment** is the basic unit of surface hydrology, the **aquifer** is the fundamental unit of groundwater hydrology.
    - Aquifers are defined by their hydraulic properties rather than strictly by geology.
    - Understanding aquifer types and properties is crucial for:
      - **Groundwater management**
      - **Well design and sustainability**
      - **Resource assessment**

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Key concept**

      An aquifer's definition depends on context—what's considered an aquifer in one region might be a confining bed in another.

# Defining an Aquifer

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      ###! An aquifer is "a lithologic unit or combination of lithologic units capable of yielding water to pumped wells or springs"
      — Domenico (1972)

    - An aquifer can be:
      - Coextensive with **geologic formations**
      - A **group of formations**
      - **Part of a formation**
      - Independent of geologic units (cutting across formations)

  .container width:{40%}
    !(100%)[Geologic formations in Grand Canyon](image/internet_grand_canyon.jpg "Geologic formations can be very complex, and Aquifers can be coextensive with them.")

# Confining Beds

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    - Units of **low permeability** that bound an aquifer are called **confining beds**.
    - The designation is **context-dependent**:
      - In areas with prolific aquifers → low permeability unit = confining bed
      - In groundwater-poor regions → same deposit might be considered an aquifer

  .container width:{50%} borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred} radius:{0.5cm}
      **Important note**

      In practice, this ambiguity is resolved by explicitly defining **hydraulic conductivity** or **porosity** values that characterise the unit.
      !(100%)[Confining Beds](image/internet_schematic_confiningbed.jpg "Confining Beds")



# Unconfined Aquifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    - Also called **water table aquifers**
    - The **water table** forms the upper boundary
    - No confining layer above
    - Wells or piezometers installed in unconfined aquifers approximately define the water table position
    - Water is under **atmospheric pressure** at the water table

  .container width:{50%}
    !(100%)[Unconfined aquifer](image/franklin_fig_4-1.png "Unconfined, confined, and perched aquifers")

# Confined Aquifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    - Also called **artesian aquifers**
    - Bounded by confining beds on **both top and bottom**
    - Water is under **pressure** greater than atmospheric
    - The water level in a well occurs **above the upper boundary** of the aquifer
    - Occasionally, water level occurs **above ground surface** (flowing artesian well)

  .container width:{50%}
    !(100%)[Confined aquifer](image/franklin_fig_4-1.png "Unconfined, confined, and perched aquifers")

# Perched Aquifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    - An **unconfined aquifer** that develops **above the regional water table**
    - Forms on top of a low hydraulic conductivity layer
    - An **unsaturated zone exists below** the perched aquifer
    - Often temporary or seasonal
    - Important for local water supply in some areas

  .container width:{50%}
    !(100%)[Perched aquifer](image/franklin_fig_4-1.png "Unconfined, confined, and perched aquifers")

    **Key feature**: Unsaturated zone both above and below the perched zone

# Comparing Aquifer Types

.fullspan
  .align{center}
    |**Aquifer Type**|**Upper Boundary**|**Lower Boundary**|**Pressure**|**Water Level**|
    |:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
    |**Unconfined**|Water table (free surface)|Confining bed or impermeable layer|Atmospheric at water table|At water table|
    |**Confined**|Confining bed|Confining bed|Above atmospheric|Above aquifer top|
    |**Perched**|Water table|Low-K layer (perching layer)|Atmospheric at water table|Above regional water table|
    "Summary of aquifer types and their characteristics"

#

.row gap:{1cm} alignment:{center}
  .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred} alignment:{center}
    ##! Types of Confining Beds

.whitespace height:{3cm}

# Different Classifications of Confining Beds

.row gap:{1cm} alignment:{center}
  .container width:{50%}
    Three terms are occasionally used to describe different types of confining beds:

    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue} alignment:{center}
      **Aquifuge**

      - The ultimate low hydraulic conductivity unit
      - **Extremely poor** conductor of groundwater
      - **No storage capacity**
      - Example: intact unfractured crystalline rock

  .container width:{50%}
    .center
        .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
          **Aquiclude**

          - Similarly **low permeability** as aquifuge
          - **Able to store water** (has porosity)
          - Transmits water very slowly
          - Example: clay layers
    .whitespace height:{0.2cm}

    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Aquitard**

      - A **low permeability unit** (leaky confining bed)
      - Can **store and transmit** water between adjacent aquifers
      - Stored water available to wells in nearby aquifers
      - Example: silty clay layers

# The Role of Aquitards

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    Aquitards play important dual roles:

    - **Influence rates of recharge** between aquifer layers
    - Can **protect underlying aquifers** from contaminants migrating downward from the ground surface
    - Act as a **barrier** to vertical contaminant transport
    - Provide **slow release** of water to adjacent aquifers during pumping

  .container width:{40%}
    !(100%)[Aquitard between two aquifers](image/internet_aquitard.jpg "Aquitard between two aquifers")

# The Complexity of Real Aquitards

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    - Detailed characterisation in the **midcontinent region of North America** shows that simple concepts don't capture reality.
    - Runkel et al. (2018) use the term **"aquitardifers"** to describe confining beds that behave **both as an aquitard and aquifer** at the same place.

  .container width:{50%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred} radius:{0.5cm}
      **Key insight**

      Real confining beds are often more complex than simple one-dimensional models suggest.

# Characteristics of Aquitardifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    **Extreme anisotropy** in hydraulic conductivity:

    - **Horizontal direction**:
      - Permeable partings **parallel to bedding**
      - Can transmit water horizontally like an aquifer

    - **Vertical direction**:
      - Layering of low permeability units
      - Sufficiently low $ K_v $ to inhibit vertical transport of contaminants

  .container width:{40%} alignment:{center}
    !(100%)[Aquitardifers](image/internet_horizontal_flow_aquitard.png "Aquitardifers")

# Additional Complexity: Fractures

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    In some shallow settings, aquitardifers develop **vertical fractures**:

    - Create **fast-flow pathways**
    - Can extend over **relatively large areas**
    - Provide direct connection between surface and deeper units
    - Completely change the protective function of the confining bed
    - Challenge simple predictions of contaminant transport

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred}
      **Management implication**

      Detailed site characterisation is essential—simple textbook models may not apply.

#
.row gap:{1cm} alignment:{center}
  .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue} alignment:{center}
    ##! Key Aquifer Properties


.whitespace height:{2cm}

# Two Important Aquifer Properties

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    When a pump is turned on in a well:

    1. Water level in the well casing (and hydraulic head) is **reduced**
    2. This causes groundwater to **flow from the aquifer into the well**
    3. Much of the pumped water initially comes from **"storage"** in the aquifer

    Therefore, aquifers have at least two important characteristics:
    - **Ability to store** groundwater
    - **Ability to transmit** this water to a nearby well

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Key concept**

      These properties depend to an important extent on the **geologic setting**.

# Transmissivity

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Definition**

      The rate at which water of prevailing kinematic viscosity is transmitted through a **unit width** of the aquifer under a **unit hydraulic gradient**.

    - Similar concept to hydraulic conductivity
    - Main difference: applies across the **vertical thickness** of an aquifer
    - Integrates conductivity over aquifer thickness

  .container width:{50%}
    !(100%)[Transmissivity concept](image/franklin_fig_4-2.png "Transmissivity and Conductivity")

# Transmissivity Equation

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    If the thickness of the aquifer is $ b $, the transmissivity $ T $ is:

    .align{center}
      .container borderwidth:{2pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue} alignment:{center} radius:{0.5cm}
        $ T = K \times b $

    Where:
    - $ T $ = transmissivity $ [L^2/T] $
    - $ K $ = hydraulic conductivity $ [L/T] $
    - $ b $ = aquifer thickness $ [L] $

    **Units**: m²/day, ft²/day, or gpd/ft (gallons per day per foot)

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred}
      **Physical meaning**

      Transmissivity tells you how much water can flow through the **entire thickness** of an aquifer per unit width.

# Darcy's Law for Aquifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    For a **homogeneous confined aquifer**, Darcy's equation can be written in terms of transmissivity:

    !(100%)[Transmissivity diagram](image/franklin_fig_3-7.png)

  .container width:{50%}
    Apply Darcy's law across the aquifer:

    $ Q = T \times W \times i $

    Where:
    - $ Q $ = discharge \[ $ L^3/T $ \]
    - $ T $ = transmissivity \[ $ L^2/T $ \]
    - $ W $ = width perpendicular to flow \[ $ L $ \]
    - $ i $ = hydraulic gradient [dimensionless]


# Storativity and Specific Storage

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    Aquifers can store water. **How this storage is accomplished differs** depending upon whether the aquifer is confined or unconfined.

    **Confined aquifer — Two mechanisms supply water**:

    1. **Water expansion**: Lower pressure → water molecules expand slightly
    2. **Aquifer compression**: Lower water pressure → less support for skeleton → grains pushed closer together → squeezes water out

  .container width:{40%}
    !(100%)[Confined aquifers and pumping](image/internet_unconfined_aquifer.png "Confined aquifer before and after pumping")

# Understanding Aquifer Compression

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{40%}
    **Before pumping**:
    - Water pressure holds grains apart
    - Aquifer skeleton is supported
    - Pore space is at maximum

    **During pumping (head declines)**:
    - Water pressure decreases
    - Weight of overlying rocks pushes down
    - Grains move closer together
    - Pore space reduces → water squeezed out

    **Result**: Only **small amounts** of water released ($ S = 10^{-5} $ to $ 10^{-3} $)

  .container width:{60%}
    !(100%)[Aquifer](image/internet_AquiferCompaction_508Blue_crop_4mg_0.gif "Aquifer compaction")


# Land Subsidence: Permanent Compression

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    When pumping is **excessive or prolonged**:
    - Initial compression is **elastic** (recoverable)
    - Continued compression becomes **plastic** (permanent)
    - Aquifer structure permanently altered
    - Land surface subsides

    **Why clay layers are critical**:
    - Clay is ~1000× more compressible than rock
    - Major contributor to subsidence
    - Once compressed, **cannot recover**

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred}
      **Real-world example**

      **Houston, Texas**:
      - Groundwater depletion from Gulf Coast aquifer
      - Land subsided **>9 ft (>2.75 m)**
      - Damage to infrastructure
      - Increased flooding risk

# Storage in Unconfined Aquifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    **Unconfined aquifer**:
    - Main source of water is **drainage of water from pores** as the water table declines
    - Much more water released per unit decline in head
    - For a comparable unit decline in hydraulic head, an unconfined aquifer releases **much more water** from storage than a confined aquifer

  .container width:{40%}
    !(100%)[Unconfined aquifer and pumping](image/internet_schematic_cross_sectional_diagram_744.webp  "Unconfined aquifer with water table dropping, water draining from pores above the new water table level")

# Storativity Definition

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    .container borderwidth:{2pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue} alignment:{center}
      **Storativity** ($ S $) is the volume of water that an aquifer releases from or takes into storage per **unit surface area** of the aquifer per **unit change in head**.

    .align{center}
      $ S = \frac{\text{volume of water}}{\text{unit area} \times \text{unit head change}} = \frac{m^3}{m^2 \times m} $

    - Dimensionless quantity
    - For **confined aquifers**: $ S $ ranges between $ 10^{-3} $ to $ 10^{-5} $
    - For **unconfined aquifers**: $ S $ (or specific yield) ranges between $ 0.01 $ to $ 0.30 $

  .container width:{50%}
    !(100%)[Storativity concept](image/franklin_fig_4-3.png "Concept of storativity and specific storage")

# Specific Storage

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Specific storage** ($ S_s $) is the volume of water that an aquifer releases from or takes into storage per **unit volume** of aquifer per **unit change in head**.

    .align{center}
      $ S_s = \frac{\text{volume of water}}{\text{unit volume} \times \text{unit head change}} $

    Units: $ [1/L] $ (e.g., $ 1/m $ or $ 1/ft $)

  .container width:{40%}
    **Relationship between $ S $ and $ S_s $:**

    .align{center}
      .container borderwidth:{2pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue} alignment:{center}
        $ S = S_s \times b $

    where $ b $ is the aquifer thickness.

# Visual Summary: Storativity

.fullspan
  .align{center}
    !(70%)[Storativity diagram](image/franklin_fig_4-3.png "Concept of storativity: confined aquifer shows small release due to water expansion and aquifer compression; unconfined aquifer shows large release due to drainage from pores")

# Comparing Storage Properties

.row gap:{1cm}
  .center
     .container width:{100%} alignment:{center}
       .center
           |**Property**|**Symbol**|**Definition**|**Units**|**Typical Values**|
           |:---|:---:|:---|:---:|:---|
           |**Specific Storage**|$ S_s $|Storage per unit volume|$ [1/L] $|$ 10^{-6} $ to $ 10^{-4} $ (1/m)|
           |**Storativity (confined)**|$ S $|Storage per unit area|Dimensionless|$ 10^{-5} $ to $ 10^{-3} $|
           |**Specific Yield (unconfined)**|$ S_y $|Drainable porosity|Dimensionless|$ 0.01 $ to $ 0.30 $|
           "Summary of aquifer storage properties"

#

.row gap:{1cm} alignment:{center}
  .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred} alignment:{center}
    ##! Mathematical Formulation of Storage

.whitespace height:{3cm}

# Specific Storage in Confined Aquifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    For a confined aquifer, specific storage reflects storage from:
    - **Compression of the granular matrix**
    - **Expansion of water**

    The mathematical definition (Domenico and Schwartz, 1998):

    .align{center}
      .container borderwidth:{2pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue} alignment:{center} radius:{0.5cm}
        $ S_s = \rho_w g (\beta_p + n\beta_w) $

  .container width:{40%}
    Where:
    - $ \rho_w $ = density of water $ [ML^{-3}] $
    - $ g $ = gravitational constant (9.81 m/sec²) $ [LT^{-2}] $
    - $ n $ = porosity of the aquifer
    - $ \beta_p $ = vertical compressibility of rock matrix
    - $ \beta_w $ = compressibility of water

# Compressibility of Water and Matrix

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    **Compressibility** ($ \beta $) quantifies how much a material compresses under pressure.

    **Units**: inverse of pressure \[$ 1/Pa $\] or \[$ m^2/N $\]

    **Key insight**:
    - **Higher** compressibility = more compressible
    - **Lower** compressibility = more rigid/incompressible

    Water compressibility ($ \beta_w $):
    - $ 4.4 \times 10^{-10} $ m²/N at 25°C

  .container width:{50%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Material property comparison**

      Clay is ~1000× more compressible than sound rock

      This is why clay layers are major contributors to land subsidence!

# Compressibility Values for Earth Materials

.fullspan
  .align{center}
    .container width:{85%}
      **Geologic Materials (matrix compressibility $ \alpha $)**

      | Material | Compressibility (m²/N) |
      |:---------|:----------------------:|
      | Clay | $ 1 \times 10^{-6} $ to $ 1 \times 10^{-8} $ |
      | Sand | $ 1 \times 10^{-7} $ to $ 1 \times 10^{-9} $ |
      | Gravel | $ 1 \times 10^{-8} $ to $ 1 \times 10^{-10} $ |
      | Jointed Rock | $ 1 \times 10^{-8} $ to $ 1 \times 10^{-10} $ |
      | Sound Rock | $ 1 \times 10^{-9} $ to $ 1 \times 10^{-11} $ |

      .whitespace height:{0.5cm}

      **Fluid compressibility $ \beta $**

      | Fluid | Compressibility (m²/N) |
      |:------|:----------------------:|
      | Water | $ 4.4 \times 10^{-10} $ |

      _Note: Loose sediments are more compressible than well-cemented rocks_

# Using the Specific Storage Equation

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    The equation $ S_s = \rho_w g (\beta_p + n\beta_w) $ can be used to estimate specific storage and storativity.

    **Example calculation**:
    - Clay layer with $ n = 0.3 $
    - $ \beta_p = 1 \times 10^{-7} $ m²/N
    - $ \beta_w = 4.4 \times 10^{-10} $ m²/N
    - $ \rho_w g \approx 10^4 $ N/m³

    $ S_s = 10^4 (1 \times 10^{-7} + 0.3 \times 4.4 \times 10^{-10}) $
    $ S_s \approx 1 \times 10^{-3} $ m⁻¹

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Key observation**

      The matrix compressibility ($ \beta_p $) term typically **dominates** over the water compressibility term, especially in fine-grained materials like clay.

# Storage in Unconfined Aquifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    In an unconfined aquifer, the groundwater response to pumping is **different** from a confined aquifer:

    **Early time** (no significant water level change):
    - Water comes from **expansion** of the water
    - Water comes from **compression** of the grains
    - Similar to confined aquifer behaviors

    **Later on** (water table falls):
    - Water mainly comes from **gravity drainage** of pores
    - This is the dominant storage mechanism

  .container width:{40%}
    !(100%)[Unconfined aquifer](image/internet_b.png "Response to reduction in hydraulic head")

# Storativity of Unconfined Aquifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    The storativity of an unconfined aquifer is expressed as:

    .align{center}
      .container borderwidth:{2pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue} alignment:{center} radius:{0.5cm}
        $ S = S_y + bS_s $

    Where:
    - $ S_y $ = specific yield of the aquifer
    - $ b $ = aquifer thickness
    - $ S_s $ = specific storage

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred}
      **Key insight**

      - Specific yield: $ 0.1 $ to $ 0.3 $
      - Product $ bS_s $: $ 10^{-3} $ to $ 10^{-5} $

      Thus, **specific yield is the dominant storage term** for unconfined aquifers.

# Aquifer Type Transitions

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{100%}
    In some cases, an aquifer may be:
    - **Confined at early stage** of pumping
    - **Becomes unconfined** at late time

    **Process**:
    1. Initial pumping creates cone of depression
    2. Water levels decline
    3. Head falls below the top of the aquifer
    4. Aquifer dewaters from the top down
    5. Storage mechanism changes from elastic to gravity drainage

    As the aquifer changes from confined to unconfined, **storativity values change accordingly**.

# Specific Yield and Specific Retention

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Specific yield** ($ S_y $) is the water released from a water-bearing material by **gravity drainage**.

    Expressed as the ratio of:

    .align{center}
      .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.3cm} background:{.lightblue} alignment:{center}
        $ S_y = \frac{V_d}{V_T} $

    Where:
    - $ V_d $ = volume of water that drains by gravity
    - $ V_T $ = total volume of soil or rock (after being saturated)

  .container width:{40%}
    <!-- Placeholder: Diagram showing saturated sample before drainage and after drainage, with water draining out under gravity, showing retained water film on grains -->

# Specific Retention

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    Not all water initially present is released from storage.

    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Specific retention** ($ S_r $) describes water that is **retained** as a film on grain surfaces or held in small openings by molecular attraction.

    .align{center}
      .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.3cm} background:{.lightblue} alignment:{center}
        $ S_r = \frac{V_r}{V_T} $

    Where:
    - $ V_r $ = volume of water retained against gravity
    - $ V_T $ = total volume of soil or rock

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred}
      **Important relationship**

      Porosity is related to specific yield and specific retention by:

      $ n = S_y + S_r $

      The sum equals the total porosity.

# Specific Retention Characteristics

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    Specific retention **increases with**:
    - **Decrease in grain size** (more surface area)
    - **Decrease in pore size** (stronger capillary forces)

    **Typical values**:
    - Coarse gravel: $ S_r \approx 0.01 $ to $ 0.05 $
    - Fine sand: $ S_r \approx 0.05 $ to $ 0.15 $
    - Silt: $ S_r \approx 0.15 $ to $ 0.30 $
    - Clay: $ S_r \approx 0.30 $ to $ 0.50 $

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Inverse relationship**

      Materials with high specific retention have **low specific yield**, and vice versa.

      This is why clay has high porosity but yields little water!

#
.whitespace height:{3cm}

.row gap:{1cm} alignment:{center}
  .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue} alignment:{center}
    ##! Examples of Real-World Aquifer Systems

# Principal Aquifers in the United States


.row gap:{1cm}
    .container width:{65%}
        !(100%)[Principal aquifers](image/franklin_fig_4-4.png )

    .container width:{35%}
        _Principal Aquifers in the United States organized by aquifer type and showing pumping rates for different uses_
        - This collection accounts for about 90% of daily groundwater production in the US.

# Aquifer Types and Their Importance

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    **Unconsolidated sand and gravel aquifers**:
    - Most extensively pumped
    - Provide much of groundwater in western US
    - High permeability and storage
    - Examples: High Plains, Central Valley, Mississippi River Valley

    **Sandstone aquifers**:
    - Important in many regions
    - Lower permeability than unconsolidated sediments
    - Can be very extensive

  .container width:{50%}
    **Carbonate-rock aquifers**:
    - Limestone and dolomite
    - Solution-enhanced permeability
    - Examples: Floridan aquifer system

    **Crystalline-rock aquifers**:
    - Fractured granite, basalt
    - Flow primarily in fractures
    - Important in New England

    **Volcanic-rock aquifers**:
    - Basalt flows with high permeability
    - Hawaiian volcanic, Columbia Plateau

# Basin-Fill Aquifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    Among the list of principal aquifers, **unconsolidated sand and gravel aquifers** rank among the most important aquifer systems in the United States.

    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Basin-fill aquifers** form when:
      - Structural basins or troughs associated with mountain ranges
      - Amplify the quantity of sediments deposited
      - Can be hundreds or thousands of meters thick

  .container width:{40%}
    <!-- Placeholder: Cross-section diagram of basin-fill aquifer showing mountain ranges on sides, thick sediment accumulation in basin center, with arrows showing sediment transport from mountains -->

# Important Basin-Fill Aquifer Systems

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{100%}
    **Basin and Range Province** (California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona):
    - Area underlain by basin-fill aquifers: ~383,000 km²
    - Associated production ranks 4th among Principal Aquifers
    - Provides water to: Las Vegas, Phoenix, Reno, Salt Lake City

    **Characteristics of Basin and Range aquifers**:
    - Long and narrow bodies
    - Sand and gravel interbedded with finer sediments (silt and clay)
    - Extensional tectonics led to formation
    - Down-faulted basins among mountain ranges
    - Some basins drained by streams; others topographically closed

# Other Notable Basin-Fill Systems

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    **Central Valley aquifer system** (California):
    - One of the world's most important aquifers
    - Extensive agricultural use
    - Major groundwater depletion issues

    **Indo-Gangetic aquifer** (Pakistan, India, Bangladesh):
    - Among top 10 of world's most important aquifers
    - Supports massive population
    - Critical for food security

  .container width:{50%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred}
      **Common characteristics**

      Basin-fill aquifers in Basin and Range tend to be:
      - Long, narrow bodies
      - Comprised of interbedded coarse and fine materials
      - Some are drained (open basins)
      - Others are topographically closed

#
.whitespace height:{3cm}

.row gap:{1cm} alignment:{center}
  .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue} alignment:{center}
    ##! Fluvial Aquifers

# Fluvial Aquifers: An Introduction

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    **Fluvial processes** are also important in creating aquifers.

    Sediments carried by rivers end up deposited in rivers, creating **fluvial deposits** that:
    - Take on the shape of river valleys
    - Typically produce aquifers that are **long, narrow, and thin**

    Boggs (1987) recognizes two main environmental settings:
    - **Meandering rivers**
    - **Braided rivers**

  .container width:{40%}
    <!-- Placeholder: Map view comparison showing meandering river with curved channels and point bars vs braided river with multiple interwoven channels -->

# Meandering Rivers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    **Characteristics**:
    - Comprised of looping, sinuous channels
    - Occupy some portion of the flood plain
    - Produce **linear shoestring sand bodies**
    - Aligned parallel to river course
    - Bounded below and on both sides by finer materials

    **Geometry**:
    - Shoestring sands are **many times wider than thick**
    - Relatively **discontinuous laterally**

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Example**

      Meandering streams like the Cant (1982) produce point bar deposits that migrate laterally as the channel moves.

# Braided Rivers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    **Braided rivers** represent **higher energy environments** with:
    - Comparatively larger flows
    - Higher sediment loads
    - Coarser sheet-like sands
    - Contain finer materials enclosed within them

    **Deposition pattern**:
    - More extensive deposition of sand
    - Function of **constant sediment deposition**

  .container width:{50%}
    !(100%)[Braided stream](image/franklin_fig_4-8.png "This braided stream in Alaska shows large sediment load under low flow conditions with expansive sand areas")

# Braided Stream Characteristics

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    Under **low flow conditions**, braided systems show:
    - Multiple channels across the riverbed
    - Evident channel network
    - Rapid sedimentation
    - Flow redistributed by constantly evolving channel network
    - Sands distributed broadly across the stream valley

    **Aquifer characteristics**:
    - More laterally continuous than meandering systems
    - Better connectivity
    - Often higher transmissivity

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred}
      **Real-world example**

      The braided stream in Alaska (Figure 4.8) shows:
      - Large sediment load
      - Expansive areas of sand between active channels
      - Typical low-flow configuration

# Meandering vs Braided: Different Environments

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    **Meandering streams** are confined more rigorously in:
    - **Narrow channels**
    - Separated by islands or bars
    - Greater sinuosity
    - Finer sediment load
    - Point bars and natural levees
    - Overbank settings or back swamps
    - Much finer silt and clay deposits

  .container width:{50%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Historical context**

      River systems in North America developed at the margins of glaciers (e.g., Ohio River) often start as **braided streams** with:
      - Large quantities of sediments
      - Meltwater from continental glaciers

      With the retreat of glaciers, streams change to become **meandering**.

# Evolution Creates Productive Aquifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{100%}
    .container borderwidth:{2pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue} radius:{0.5cm}
      **Key insight**

      Sediments associated with braided streams typically create the **most productive alluvial aquifers**.

    **Why braided stream deposits are better aquifers**:
    - More continuous laterally
    - Coarser grain size (higher K)
    - Greater thickness
    - Better hydraulic connectivity
    - Less fine-grained material

    **Examples**: High Plains aquifer, Mississippi River Valley alluvial aquifer

#
.whitespace height:{3cm}

.row gap:{1cm} alignment:{center}
  .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred} alignment:{center}
    ##! Aquifers in Semi-consolidated Sediments

# Semi-consolidated Sand Aquifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    This family of aquifers is **semi-consolidated sand interbedded with**:
    - Silt
    - Clay
    - Minor carbonate rocks

    **Where they are found**:
    - Formed in coastal settings
    - Shallow fluvial, and shallow marine environments
    - Associated with **coastal plains** along Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Key characteristic**

      These aquifers are **partially consolidated** — intermediate between unconsolidated sediments and fully lithified rocks.

# Gulf Coast Aquifer Systems

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{100%}
    USGS has identified several aquifer systems along the Gulf Coast:

    1. **Coastal lowlands aquifer system** (Texas)
    2. **Mississippi embayment aquifer system** (Arkansas, Louisiana)
    3. **Texas coastal uplands aquifer system**
    4. **Southeastern Coastal Plain aquifer system**
    5. **Northern Atlantic Coastal Plain aquifer system**

.fullspan
  .align{center}
    !(85%)[Gulf Coast aquifers](image/franklin_fig_4-16.png "Major aquifer systems of the Gulf Coastal plains shown with Mississippi River Valley alluvial aquifer")

# Characteristics of Gulf Coast Aquifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    These aquifers typically **crop out in topographically higher areas** where they are unconfined.

    **Moving seaward**:
    - Become confined with upward leakage to shallow aquifers
    - Discharge to saltwater bodies
    - Flow is sluggish near the ends of long regional flow systems
    - Aquifers commonly contain **unflushed saline water** in deeply buried, downdip parts

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred}
      **Saltwater intrusion risk**

      When shallow aquifers are pumped near coasts, saltwater intrusion can lead to **salinization** of groundwater. The Mississippi River Valley alluvial aquifer overlies older rocks in the Mississippi embayment.

# Cross Section of Coastal Lowlands Aquifer

.fullspan
  .align{center}
    !(95%)[Cross section](image/franklin_fig_4-17.png "Cross section showing unconsolidated units comprising the Coastal lowlands aquifer system in Texas with confining units")

    _Units thicken toward the Gulf of Mexico. Subsidence has accommodated uplift on uplands wedge-shaped geometries._

# Aquifer Properties: Gulf Coast System

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{50%}
    The Coastal lowlands aquifer system consists of **five aquifer units** (Permeable Units A through E) and **two confining beds** (Zone D and Zone E confining units).

    **Typical characteristics**:
    - Units thicken toward Gulf of Mexico
    - Subsidence in Gulf Basin from weight of sediments
    - Wedge-shaped geometry

  .container width:{50%}
    **Storage and transmission properties**:

    - **Where confined**: storativity between $ 10^{-4} $ to $ 10^{-3} $
    - **Where unconfined**: specific yield values from 10% to 30%
    - **Hydraulic conductivity**: $ 17-21 $ ft/day (or $ 5-7 $ m/day)
    - **Transmissivity**: $ 5000 $ to $ 35000 $ ft²/day (or $ 500-4000 $ m²/day)

# Case Study: Houston Groundwater Depletion

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    **Fifty percent of total withdrawals** from the aquifer system in 1985 was concentrated in and around Houston.

    **Production sources**:
    - Permeable units A, B, and C

    **Large withdrawals of groundwater** by 1982 produced:
    - **300-ft (91-m) decline** in Permeable Zone B
    - **>400 ft (121 m) decline** in Zone C

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred}
      **Land subsidence consequence**

      The large declines in water levels contributed to **land subsidence** in the Houston area:

      More than **9 ft (>2.75 m)** of subsidence (Ryder, 1996).

#
.whitespace height:{3cm}

.row gap:{1cm} alignment:{center}
  .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue} alignment:{center}
    ##! Sandstone Aquifers

# Sandstone Aquifers: Introduction

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    **Sandstone** is a rock formed from cementation of sand.

    **Key characteristics**:
    - Typically retains only a **small fraction** of the primary porosity of sand
    - Compaction and cementation together cause **substantial reduction** in porosity
    - **Secondary openings** (joints, fractures, bedding-plane partings) facilitate flow
    - Hydraulic conductivity: **low to moderate**
    - Can provide **large quantities of water** because they extend over large areas

  .container width:{40%}
    <!-- Placeholder: Block diagram showing sandstone with primary porosity between grains plus secondary openings (fractures and bedding planes) -->

# Important Sandstone Aquifers

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{100%}
    Sandstone aquifers are common across the United States and include:

    - **Colorado Plateau** aquifer systems
    - **Denver Basin** aquifer system
    - **Lower Cretaceous aquifers** (Northern Great Plains aquifer system)
    - Many others too numerous to mention

    .whitespace height:{0.5cm}

    **Focus of this section**:
    - Dakota Sandstone aquifer (Northern Great Plains)
    - Nubian sandstone (North Africa)

# Dakota Sandstone Aquifer

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    The **Dakota Sandstone** is notable for:
    - Many studies through the years
    - One of the **earliest understood** artesian aquifers
    - Important role in **confining beds** play

    **Classic artesian aquifer studies**:
    - Chamberlin (1885)
    - Darton (1909)

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Historical significance**

      Early studies of "classical" artesian aquifers included the Dakota Sandstone and contributed to fundamental understanding of confined aquifer systems.

# Dakota Aquifer System Structure

.fullspan
  .align{center}
    !(90%)[Dakota cross section](image/franklin_fig_4-18.png "West-east cross section showing the most important aquifers and confining beds comprising the Dakota aquifer system")

    _The aquifer system stretches from Black Hills eastward under entire state of South Dakota_

# Characteristics of Classic Artesian Aquifer

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    **The aquifer itself** is confined by:
    - Rocks of much lower permeability
    - **Cretaceous shale** below
    - Structural deformation/erosion of rocks led to exposure in uplands
    - **Direct recharge** occurs in upland areas

    **Potentiometric surface**:
    - Might occur **above ground surface** where aquifer is topographically lower
    - Initially, before extensive pumping impacts

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred}
      **Important concept**

      This simple model assumes flow is mostly **through the aquifer** with:
      - No flow in beds below
      - Only minor leakage upward

      However, both Chamberlin and Darton appreciated that **flow was possible through confining beds**.

# Dakota Aquifer System Components

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{100%}
    Three major aquifers present in the basin:

    1. **Mississippian carbonate rocks** (Madison Group)
    2. **Inyan Kara Group Sandstones**
    3. **Newcastle Sandstone**

    These aquifers **crop out on the eastern flank** of the Black Hills.

    **Confining beds** are largely shale and include:
    - **Madison Group confining layer**
    - **Skull Creek shale**
    - **Cretaceous Shale confining layer**

# Flow Patterns in Dakota Aquifer

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    Studies showed the aquifer systems behaved **much differently** than the classic conceptual model of a completely confined aquifer.

    **Total inflows and outflow** through entire aquifer in South Dakota was estimated at **80 ft³/sec**.

    **In terms of recharge**, only ~25% was associated with:
    - Upland outcrops of sandstone units (Newcastle Sandstone and Inyan Kara Group)

  .container width:{40%}
    **Recharge to Madison Group**: ~29% ended up as **flux in the sandstone aquifer** because of **cross-formational flow** at depth.

    **Surprisingly**: Nearly **half the total flow** in the aquifer (~46%) came as **recharge through the Cretaceous shale confining unit**.

# Vertical Leakage Through Confining Beds

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    Although the **vertical hydraulic conductivity was low**, this unit covers a **large area** of South Dakota.

    **Flow modelling results** (Bredehoeft et al., 1983):

    - $ K_z $ value of $ 2 \times 10^{-11} $ ft/sec for combined Cretaceous shale confining layer
    - $ K_{xy} $ values:
      - Inyan Kara Group: $ 9.6 \times 10^{-5} $ ft/sec
      - Dakota-Newcastle: $ 6.4 \times 10^{-5} $ ft/sec
      - Madison Limestone: $ 1 \times 10^{-5} $ ft/sec

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Key insight**

      Most of the outflow (~80%) left the Dakota Sandstone through **upper confining bed**, rather than the eastern end of the aquifer.

      Wells in the aquifer typically yielded 50–500 gpm.

#
.whitespace height:{3cm}

.row gap:{1cm} alignment:{center}
  .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred} alignment:{center}
    ##! Carbonate-Rock Aquifers

# Carbonate-Rock Aquifers: Introduction

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    Most of the developed carbonate aquifers supplying groundwater in the United States are found in the **east**, particularly in **Florida**.

    **Major systems**:
    - **Floridan aquifer system** (most famous)
    - **Biscayne aquifer**

    Most carbonate-rock aquifers are **limestone**, but locally:
    - **Dolomite** yields water
    - **Marble** yields water

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Wide variability**

      Water-yielding properties of carbonate rocks vary widely:
      - Some units yield **almost no water** (act as confining units)
      - Others are among the **most productive aquifers** known

# Enhancement of Permeability by Dissolution

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    Most carbonate rocks originate as **sedimentary deposits in marine environments**.

    **Post-depositional processes**:
    - Compaction
    - Cementation
    - Dolomitisation

    These greatly change **porosity and hydraulic conductivity**.

    **Most important change**: Rock dissolution by circulating, slightly acidic groundwater
    - Enlarges pore spaces
    - Creates joints, fractures, and bedding-plane partings
    - Leads to **increased hydraulic conductivity and porosity**

  .container width:{40%}
    <!-- Placeholder: Diagram showing progressive dissolution of carbonate rock - starting with intact rock with small fractures, progressing to enlarged fractures and conduits, ending with cave development -->

# Solution Conduits and Caves

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    In some cases, **solution conduits or caves** can develop that:
    - Connect recharge areas to discharge areas at the downstream end
    - Term **"solution conduit"** refers to **long openings** enlarged by groundwater
    - Such openings are generally considered to be **smaller than caves**

    Where they are saturated, carbonate rocks with **well-connected networks** of solution openings yield:
    - **Large amounts of water** to wells that penetrate the openings
    - Intact rock between secondary openings is **poorly permeable**

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred}
      **Important distinction**

      Although intact rock is poorly permeable, the **network of solution openings** creates very high bulk permeability for the aquifer as a whole.

# Conditions for Solution Enhancement

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{100%}
    Major **solutional enhancement** of permeability in carbonate aquifers depends on the circulation of groundwater.

    **Three conditions** must be present (Stringfield and LeGrande, 1966):

    1. **Chemically aggressive groundwater** must be available to recharge the system
    2. **Fractures** need to be present to transmit water
    3. **Groundwater must be able to drain out** of the system

    Commonly, these three conditions develop in **unconfined carbonate aquifers**.

# Development of Solution Conduits

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    **Creation of conduits** begins as water enlarges discontinuities close to the recharge area of the flow system.

    **Initial stage**:
    - Flow pathways develop
    - Aggressive flows rapidly through rock to discharge point
    - Conduits are only about **1 cm wide**

    **As flow paths lengthen** (kilometres):
    - Selected conduits grow to **size of caves**
    - Conduits accessible to humans
    - Extensive literature related to exploring caves

  .container width:{40%}
    !(100%)[Solution enhancement](image/franklin_fig_4-19.png "Solution enhancement of original porosity showing zones of fracture concentration")

    _Highest well yields occur where multiple fractures intersect_

# Hydraulic Conductivity Ranges in Carbonates

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    Apart from network of conduits and caves, other **secondary porosity** can be present but **not enlarged**.

    **Result**: Significant regions of a carbonate aquifer might have:
    - Hydraulic conductivities and porosities **comparable to fractured rocks**

    **Important facts** about carbonate rocks (Brahana et al., 1988):

    1. "Carbonate rocks serve as **significant aquifers throughout North America**. They are not limited by location or the age of the formation."

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Remarkable range**

      2. "Carbonate rocks show a **total range of hydraulic conductivity of 10 orders of magnitude**, from the tightest confining beds to the most prolific aquifers."

# When Carbonates Don't Develop High Permeability

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    Not all carbonate rocks develop **solution-enhanced porosity and permeability**.

    **Reasons for low permeability**:
    - Carbonate rocks are of **low permeability** and are thick
    - Carbonate rock was **never elevated** into an active groundwater circulation system
    - Features of carbonate rock **inhibit enhancement** in permeability

  .container width:{40%}
    **Examples of inhibiting features**:
    - Example: the **rock did not develop** in a carbonate rock that is essentially **unfractured**
    - Carbonate rock like **chalk** can be so porous that flow is **diffuse** and **not concentrated** along preferential paths

    In these cases, **pores grow equally**.

# Hydrogeologic Response of Carbonates

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{100%}
    3. "The hydrogeologic response of carbonates at any time is related to the **rock permeability**, which is affected most by the **dynamic process** of dynamic freshwater circulation and solution of the rock."

    4. "The significant control of the dynamic freshwater circulation is the **integrity of the hydraulic circuit**, which requires that recharge, flow-through, and discharge must be maintained. Without each of these, the system is essentially static and does not act as a conduit. Its evolution rate approaches that of noncarbonate rocks. **Secondary controls** on dynamic circulation include lithologic, structural, geomorphic, hydrologic, and chronologic aspects."

    5. "The significant controls on the process of solution are (a) **rock solubility**, and (b) the **chemical character of the groundwater**......"

#
.whitespace height:{3cm}

.row gap:{1cm} alignment:{center}
  .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} radius:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue} alignment:{center}
    ##! Karst Landscapes

# Karst Landscapes

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    Extensive modifications to carbonate or easily dissolvable rocks have a **significant influence on the landscape**.

    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Karst** describes landscapes shaped by **dissolution processes** to provide unique landforms and underground drainage.

    **Associated landforms**:
    - Sinkholes
    - Sinking streams
    - Dry valleys
    - Caves
    - Large springs

  .container width:{40%}
    <!-- Placeholder: 3D diagram of karst landscape showing surface sinkholes, disappearing streams, underground cave systems, and springs emerging at lower elevations -->

# Sinkholes

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    **Sinkholes** are bowl-shaped depressions on the land surface.

    **Formation processes**:
    - **Dissolution** and **suffusion**
    - Term **"suffusion"** refers to situation where unconsolidated surface deposits overlying bedrock are transported into karst features that form deep sinkholes
    - Unlike catastrophic collapse, **suffusion is a relatively slow process**

    **Factors affecting formation**:
    - Character of overburden materials
    - Their thickness
    - Types of materials

  .container width:{40%}
    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightred}
      **Three types of sinkholes** in Florida (Galloway et al., 1999):

      (i) **Dissolution**
      (ii) **Cover subsidence**
      (iii) **Cover-collapse** sinkholes

# Stream Sinks

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{60%}
    In the setting of shallow carbonate rocks with dissolution features, **stream sinks** can form.

    .container borderwidth:{1pt} padding:{0.5cm} background:{.lightblue}
      **Stream sinks** are places where a small stream simply **disappears into the subsurface** to follow a connected cave system before rejoining the surface water as a spring.

  .container width:{40%}
    <!-- Placeholder: Cross-section showing stream flowing on surface, then disappearing into sinkhole, flowing through underground cave system, and emerging as spring downstream -->

# Karst Features: Comprehensive View

.fullspan
  .align{center}
    !(95%)[Karst conceptual model](image/franklin_fig_4-20.png "Conceptual model showing landforms and features associated with karst including sinkholes, stream sinks, blind valleys, caves, fractures, and springs")

    _Carbonate bedrock is overlain by surficial deposits with various types of dissolution features_

# Capture and Transmission by Karst Systems

.row gap:{1cm}
  .container width:{100%}
    The ability of **fracture and cave systems** to capture and transmit surface water in various ways sometimes leads to:

    - **Absence of surface water** in dry valleys
    - Water associated with **large springs systems**

    **Various types of sinkholes** described with several classification systems:

    Galloway et al. (1999) described the types found in Florida:
    - (i) **Dissolution**
    - (ii) **Cover subsidence**
    - (iii) **Cover-collapse** sinkholes

    Each type forms through different processes and at different rates.

# Summary

.align{center}
  .container width:{75%}
    .box title:{Key takeaways from this lecture:} background:{.lightblue}
      **Aquifer Classification:**
      - Aquifers are the fundamental unit of groundwater hydrology
      - Three types: **unconfined**, **confined**, **perched**—each with distinct boundary conditions
      - Confining beds range from impermeable (aquifuge) to leaky (aquitard), with complex real-world **aquitardifers**

      **Aquifer Properties:**
      - **Transmissivity** ($ T = Kb $) quantifies ease of transmission; **storativity** ($ S $) quantifies storage release
      - Storage mechanisms: elastic ($ S_s $) in confined, gravity drainage ($ S_y $) in unconfined aquifers
      - Relationship: $ n = S_y + S_r $ connects porosity to drainable and retained water

      **Real-World Aquifer Systems:**
      - **Basin-fill** (Basin and Range): structural basins with thick sediment accumulation
      - **Fluvial**: braided streams create more continuous aquifers than meandering systems
      - **Semiconsolidated** (Gulf Coast): wedge-shaped geometry, saltwater intrusion risk, land subsidence issues
      - **Sandstone** (Dakota): vertical leakage through confining beds dominates recharge (~46%)
      - **Carbonate-rock**: solution enhancement creates 10 orders of magnitude range in hydraulic conductivity
      - **Karst landscapes**: dissolution features create unique surface and subsurface drainage systems

      Understanding aquifer diversity enables effective groundwater management and resource protection.
